reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: An acute or subacute inflammatory myelopathy producing bilateral motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction below the level of the lesion
A clearly demarcated sensory level, with bladder and bowel involvement, is a key clue to a spinal cord process rather than a peripheral one
Rapidly evolving cord compression must be excluded urgently with imaging, because it may be surgically treatable and demands emergency intervention
Longitudinally extensive lesions spanning three or more vertebral segments should raise suspicion of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and prompt aquaporin-4 antibody testing
It may be idiopathic/post-infectious or the presenting event of multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, MOG-associated disease, or a systemic autoimmune disorder
MRI of the cord with contrast and cerebrospinal fluid analysis are central to diagnosis and to identifying the underlying cause
High-dose corticosteroids are the usual first-line treatment, with plasma exchange considered for severe or steroid-refractory cases
Identifying whether the episode is monophasic or part of a relapsing disorder guides long-term immunotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Transverse myelitis is focal inflammation of the spinal cord causing demyelination and axonal injury across one or more segments, disrupting ascending sensory and descending motor tracts as well as autonomic pathways. It may follow infection or vaccination as a para- or post-infectious immune response, arise from autoimmune demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, or MOG antibody disease, or occur with systemic autoimmune conditions. Breakdown of the blood-cord barrier and inflammatory cell infiltration produce cord swelling and dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Compressive myelopathy from disc, tumour, abscess, or haematoma
Spinal cord infarction (anterior spinal artery syndrome)
Nutritional or metabolic myelopathy such as B12 deficiency
Guillain-Barre syndrome when presenting with ascending weakness
additionalInvestigations: Urgent MRI of the spine with and without contrast to exclude compression and define the inflammatory lesion
MRI of the brain to assess for demyelinating lesions suggesting multiple sclerosis
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, and infective studies
Autoimmune and infective serology, and vitamin B12, as guided by the clinical picture
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness with a sensory level and sphincter disturbance requiring emergency MRI to exclude compressive cord lesions amenable to surgery
Ascending deficit approaching the cervical cord threatening respiratory function
New bladder or bowel dysfunction and saddle sensory loss indicating significant cord involvement
Fever and back pain with neurological deficit suggesting epidural abscess as a surgical emergency
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and depends on cause, severity, and rapidity of onset. Some patients recover substantially, while others are left with significant residual deficits. Recurrent disease and poorer recovery are more typical of NMOSD and longitudinally extensive lesions, underscoring the importance of accurate aetiological diagnosis and timely immunotherapy.
pitfalls: Delaying MRI and missing a compressive lesion that requires emergency decompression
Failing to test for aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies and misclassifying the disorder
Attributing the presentation to a peripheral cause and overlooking the sensory level and cord signs
Not investigating for an infective cause before or alongside immunosuppression when indicated
management: Exclude compressive myelopathy urgently with spinal MRI, as it may be a surgically treatable emergency
Treat the acute inflammatory attack with high-dose intravenous corticosteroids (methylprednisolone)
Escalate to plasma exchange in steroid-refractory or severe cases

Direct treatment at the underlying cause: maintenance immunosuppression for aquaporin-4-positive NMOSD and MOG-antibody disease, disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis, and specific treatment of any infective or systemic autoimmune trigger
Supportive care for the neurogenic bladder and bowel, pressure-area protection, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, and management of neuropathic pain and spasticity
Early multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy and occupational therapy
Long-term relapse-prevention immunotherapy and neurology follow-up for relapsing disorders such as NMOSD
